title: Real World, Long Term Data On Cannabis Impact On Traffic Fatalities

content_html_sanitized:
Recently, I have reported on the latest Prohibitionist propaganda extravaganza from a number of media outlets about a study showing how many drivers in fatal automobile crashes had cannabis in their systems in post mortem blood tests.

See

The Editorial Page of the Wall Street Journal Degrades Itself

and links

 

As intended, it sounded terrible. Of course, that’s all that matters to Prohibitionists. The first problem was that they did not mention that most of the drivers also had other drugs in their systems, especially including alcohol. It was not explicitly stated. That certainly didn’t bother The Wall Street Journal, a publication valued precisely because it reports important details.

 

In fact, many alcoholics and polydrug users also use cannabis to help deal with their addictions, which necessarily muddles cause and effect.

See The Paradox of Cannabis Self Medication

 

Let me refer you to a study published by the National Institute of Medicine, THE EFFECT OF CANNABIS COMPARED WITH ALCOHOL ON DRIVING.

This is a very thorough report, citing a wide variety of studies, but they concluded that the data is inconclusive.

 

“Because of these difficulties, epidemiological studies have also shown inconsistent effects, some finding decreased or no risk from driving while smoking marijuana, and others increased risk. Most studies are fraught with methodological problems that could lead to underreporting of drug use or misclassification of experimental subjects into or out of the marijuana-using category, confounding results. In contrast, epidemiological studies on the relationship between alcohol consumption and accidents have been clear-cut and consistent, demonstrating that the risk of a motor vehicle accident increases significantly with BAC > 0.05%.”

 

However, as promised, there are real world data actually demonstrating that increased cannabis use is “linked to” long term declines in automobile fatalities.

From PREVALENCE OF CANNABIS USE IN THE UNITED STATES (1975–2014)

“The prevalence of cannabis use peaked in the late 1970s, when more than one-third of high school seniors (37 percent in 1976) and one in eight Americans over 12 years old (12.8 percent in 1979) reported past-month use (Johnston et al., 2016). Self-reported past-month use declined throughout the 1980s and by 1992 was just one-third of the 1970s peak, both among high school seniors (12.1 percent) and the general population (4.4 percent).”

 

(1992 was the year that I became NORML National Director, but that may be just a coincidence.)

 

Today, according to Gallup “Fifteen percent of Americans report they smoke marijuana, according to combined Gallup data from 2023 and 2024.”

 

In the U.S. traffic fatalities per 100 million miles traveled in 1993 , were 4.12. Thirty years later, U.S. fatalities per million miles traveled were down to 1.27, while marijuana use more than tripled, from 4.4% to 15%

 

Now, let me make very clear that do not think that this drop was caused (solely) by the increase in cannabis consumption, but it certainly undermines the argument for keeping cannabis in the black market, or arresting hundreds of thousands of Americans every year.

 

Of course, I oppose making smoking weed mandatory for drivers. Unlike the Editors of the Wall Street Journal, I actually believe in freedom.

 

The historical data they never want to report. From NORML: “Marijuana arrests peaked in the United States in 2007, when police made over 870,000 marijuana-related arrests. At that time, just under half (48 percent) of all drug-related arrests in the United States were for marijuana-related violations.”
